ABSTRACT Few-shot fine-grained image classification requires distinguishing visually similar categories
from only 1–5 labeled examples per class, a regime in which convolutional neural networks and vision
transformers face inherent limitations in efficiency or receptive-field coverage. State space models (SSMs),
particularly Mamba with its input-dependent selective mechanism, offer global receptive fields with linear
complexity. However, existing vision SSMs process single images in isolation, and recent attempts to bring
SSMs to few-shot learning employ them only as frozen backbones or prototype enhancers, leaving the scan
mechanism itself unexplored as a relational operator. We propose SSM-Match, which recasts the selective
scan as a cross-image matching operator: for each class, support and query patch tokens are concatenated
with a class-conditional prior token and per-image separators, and a bidirectional selective scan yields
support-conditioned query evidence and query-conditioned support summaries, fused by input-dependent
direction and evidence gates. Independent matching modules at three token-grid resolutions capture both
coarse, semantics and fine-grained detail On CUB-200-2011 5-way 5-shot, SSM-Match with a frozen
Vim-Tiny backbone reaches 84.72%, and it consistently improves over a cosine-similarity classifier on the
same features on miniImageNet, Stanford Cars, and cross-domain CIFAR-FS. With linear O(KL) matching
complexity, training completes on a single consumer GPU in approximately three hours, bringing relational
reasoning with state space models to data-efficient visual recognition.

optimization-based and metric-based paradigms. Optimization-
based approaches, exemplified by MAML [13], learn model
initializations that can rapidly adapt to new tasks through few
gradient steps. While conceptually elegant, these methods
incur the computational cost of second-order optimization
and remain susceptible to overfitting in extremely low-data

dominant paradigm due to their simplicity and effectiveness.

C. VISION STATE SPACE MODELS
Several architectures have adapted Mamba for visual tasks.
Vim [8] introduces bidirectional scanning with position em-
bedding for image classification, achieving ViT-competitive
accuracy with fewer parameters. VMamba [9] proposes a
cross-scan with four-directional scanning to capture 2D spa-
tial structure more effectively. LocalMamba [10] decomposes
images into local windows with scanning within each win-
dow, improving locality. For segmentation, SegMamba [23]
adapts the architecture for dense prediction. A comprehen-
sive survey [12] catalogs these developments and explicitly
identifies few-shot learning as an under-explored application
area.
Critically, all of these architectures process single images
in isolation. A growing body of work subsequently applies
SSMs to low-shot regimes, but always in a backbone or
feature-enhancement role: Misra et al. [28] study the low-shot
transferability of frozen V-Mamba features; VMAPN couples
a Vision Mamba encoder with enhanced prototype aggrega-
tion [29]; a Mamba–wavelet multi-scale model targets few-
shot fine-grained classification [30]; Mamba-FSCIL adapts
selective SSMs to few-shot class-incremental learning [31];
and Mamba variants have been applied to few-shot action
recognition [32] and few-shot detection/segmentation [34],
[35]. In all of these methods the scan remains confined to
one input sequence, and cross-image matching is performed
afterwards by external prototypes or distance metrics. To the
best of our knowledge, SSM-Match is the first method to
repurpose the selective scan itself as a cross-image match-
ing operator that jointly processes support and query tokens
within a single state space, moving from single-sequence
modeling to multi-sequence relational reasoning.

Why FRN can outperform SSM-Match. FRN couples a
fully trainable ResNet-12 (12.4M trained parameters) with a
feature-reconstruction head, whereas SSM-Match freezes the
backbone and trains only the matching modules. FRN’s ad-
vantage is therefore expected in settings dominated by generic
discriminative features—most notably miniImageNet, where
it leads in our comparison. On fine-grained CUB-200 5-
shot, where part-level cross-image correspondence matters
most, SSM-Match surpasses FRN while training roughly an
order of magnitude fewer parameters and matching at linear
complexity. We thus position SSM-Match as an accuracy–
efficiency trade-off under a frozen-backbone budget, not as
an absolute-accuracy claim; the equal-protocol rows make the
underlying capacity difference explicit.

ular strength. At 5-shot on CUB-200, SSM-Match achieves

their respective published settings, including DN4, Deep-
EMD, and FRN. On Stanford Cars 5-shot, SSM-Match

hypothesis that selective scanning is particularly effective for
subtle inter-class discrimination, where context-dependent
feature weighting is most valuable.

B. RELATIONSHIP TO THE ‘‘GOOD EMBEDDING’’
HYPOTHESIS
Tian et al. [5] argued that a strong feature embedding alone
can match or exceed sophisticated meta-learning algorithms.
Our results both support and refine this hypothesis. A frozen
Vim-Tiny backbone with simple cosine similarity (55.21% on
miniImageNet 1-shot) indeed provides a competitive baseline
that exceeds several Conv-4-based metric-learning methods.
However, the cross-image SSM matching module contributes
an additional 6.14% absolute gain, suggesting that both good
features and task-adaptive relational reasoning matter for
optimal few-shot performance. SSMs provide a uniquely ef-
ficient mechanism to achieve the latter without sacrificing
the former: the linear complexity allows sophisticated cross-
image reasoning at a computational cost comparable to sim-
ple fixed-distance metrics.
C. BRIDGING TWO RESEARCH COMMUNITIES
A broader contribution of this work is an early instantiation of
SSM-based relational reasoning for episodic few-shot clas-
sification. The SSM community has concentrated on single-
sequence modeling tasks—language modeling, single-image
classification, and medical image segmentation [23]—and
recent SSM excursions into low-shot vision use the archi-
tecture as a backbone or feature enhancer [28]– [32], while
the few-shot learning community has relied almost entirely
on CNNs and Transformers. By showing that cross-image
selective scanning is feasible and effective across multiple
benchmarks and settings, we hope to invite contributions from
both sides: SSM researchers can explore multi-sequence in-
teraction mechanisms beyond single-image processing, while
FSL researchers gain access to an architectural option with
favorable scaling properties—global receptive fields at linear
cost.

that current SSM backbones would benefit from larger-scale
pretraining or hybrid CNN–SSM designs that combine the in-
ductive bias of convolutions with the long-range modeling of
selective scans. Second, we have not systematically analyzed
